**Nearest-point projection.** There is a nearest-point projection map κ : Ω → Pl(Z) that sends z ∈ Ω to the first point on Pl(Z) that is touched by an expanding family of horoballs in H³ based at z. Convexity of Pl(Z) ensures that this point is well-defined. In fact, from each z ∈ Ω we obtain not just a nearest point on Pl(Z), but also a support plane H_z which contains κ(z) and whose normal vector at that point defines a geodesic ray with ideal endpoint z. This gives a map κ̂ : Ω → H^{2,1}, where H^{2,1} is the space of planes in H³ (the de Sitter space).

The canonical stratification of Ω is the decomposition into fibers of the map κ̂. Strata are of two types:

- 1-dimensional strata—circular arcs that map homeomorphically by κ onto bending lines of Pl(Z), and
- 2-dimensional strata—regions with nonempty interior bounded by circular arcs which map homeomorphically by κ to the totally geodesic pieces of Pl(Z).

Meg realizes the wounds don’t really fit a normal animal attack, while Marks increasingly finds himself out of his depth. As they follow the evidence, it becomes apparent that something supernatural may be involved.

## Discussion

I really liked the procedural angle of The Cycle. For long stretches, it feels like a television procedural, and I mean that as a compliment. It reminded me of some strange combination of Bones, CSI, and Supernatural. Meg approaches what is happening as a scientist. She studies bodies, wounds, decomposition, and physical evidence, looking for a rational explanation even as the evidence becomes increasingly irrational.

That grounding is important because the movie never immediately throws up its hands and says, “Well, it must be supernatural.” Meg tries to make the evidence fit the world she understands. Even when the supernatural elements begin working their way into the story, some of the explanations remain connected to science and forensic investigation. That gives the movie a different feel from a lot of supernatural horror.

What I also liked is the particular direction the supernatural side of the story eventually takes. I don’t want to say too much because discovering exactly what Meg is dealing with is part of the fun. The film takes something very old and familiar from horror and approaches it through modern forensic science. Instead of simply accepting folklore and legend, Meg looks at wounds, physical changes, decomposition, and other evidence and tries to explain what she is seeing scientifically. It is an interesting way to approach a piece of horror mythology that we have all seen many times before.

There is also something effective about watching a scientist slowly run out of rational explanations. Meg knows what an animal attack looks like. She knows what happens to a human body after death. Those are things she can measure and understand. But what happens when the evidence tells her that the thing she is looking for doesn’t fit comfortably into either category? The Cycle has a lot of fun living in that space between science and folklore.

New inhomogeneous Bismut Hermitian-Einstein threefolds with large symmetry group

Fabio Podestà, Alberto Raffero

arXiv:2610.37102

Authors: Fabio Podestà, Alberto Raffero

Submitted: Oct 2026 | Updated: Oct 2026

We study compact non-Kähler Bismut Hermitian-Einstein threefolds whose connected full group of holomorphic isometries acts with cohomogeneity one. We prove that the Lie algebra of this group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3\oplus\mathfrak{su}(2)$ or $\mathbb{R}^2\oplus\mathfrak{su}(2)$, unless the Bismut connection is flat. We then focus on the first case, where we determine the possible singular isotropy algebras and reduce the Bismut Hermitian-Einstein condition to a system of ordinary differential equations. We obtain explicit solutions satisfying suitable smoothness conditions, that yield families of compact and complete non-compact non-Kähler Bismut Hermitian-Einstein threefolds with non-constant scalar curvature and non-zero Bismut curvature, including examples on $S^3\times S^3$ and $S^3\times S^1\times\mathbb{R}^2$, respectively. We also investigate the topology of the compact examples and determine the asymptotic scalar curvature of the non-compact ones. Moreover, we prove the existence of a smooth deformation of a Bismut-flat Samelson structure on $S^3\times S^3$ through non-Kähler Bismut Hermitian-Einstein structures that are not Bismut-flat. The regularity of the constructed compact examples is also investigated.

Constant Chern holomorphic sectional curvature on two-step solvmanifolds

Shanlin Guan, Yuqin Guo

arXiv:2610.34820

Authors: Shanlin Guan, Yuqin Guo

Submitted: Oct 2026 | Updated: Oct 2026

Let $M=Γ\backslash G$ be a compact solvmanifold with a left-invariant Hermitian structure whose Lie algebra is two-step solvable. If the Chern holomorphic sectional curvature is constant, then the derived algebra is $J$-invariant and the Chern connection is flat. At the Lie-algebra level, we also prove that constant Chern holomorphic sectional curvature is impossible for a unimodular two-step solvable Hermitian Lie algebra of mixed Freibert-Swann type.

## Abstract

We use supernatural bundles to build $\mathbf{GL}$ -equivariant resolutions supported on the diagonal of $\mathbb{P}^{n}\times \mathbb{P}^{n}$ , in a way that extends Beilinson’s resolution of the diagonal. We thus obtain results about supernatural bundles that largely parallel known results about exceptional collections. We apply this construction to Boij–Söderberg decompositions of cohomology tables of vector bundles, yielding a proof of concept for the idea that those positive rational decompositions should admit meaningful categorifications.

#### 6.3.4 POINT TO CONVEX POLYGON

In the special case of a convex polygon, not all point-to-segment tests need to be made while searching for the minimum distance between the point and edges of the polygon. Only those edges that are visible to the point X must be considered. Figure 6.13 illustrates the idea.

Image

Figure 6.13. Only those edges visible to the test point must be searched for the closest point to the test point. The three visible edges are dotted. The invisible edges are drawn in black. The visible edges are in a cone with vertex at the test point and whose sides are tangent to the convex polygon.

Assuming that each edge 〈{P}_{i},{P}_{i+1}〉 has an associated normal vector {\overrightarrow{n}}_{i} that points to the interior of the polygon, an edge is visible only if {\overrightarrow{n}}_{i}·\left(X-{P}_{i}\right)\ge 0. By testing this dot product first, and if negative, the potential division that occurs in the point-to-segment distance calculation is avoided. Moreover, a further reduction in calculations is attained by checking if the next point-to-segment distance is larger than the current one. If the distance to the current edge is smaller or equal to the distance from the two neighboring edges, then the current distance is the minimum distance to the polygon boundary.

Finally, given a point and a convex polygon, the GJK algorithm described in Section 6.10 provides a viable alternative to a boundary search algorithm that looks for a closest feature. The method extends to higher dimensions and to arbitrary convex objects, not necessarily polygons or polyhedra.
